newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police warn Zajedno as court appeal fails.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police warn Zajedno as court appeal fails.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties lost their legal battle for control of Belgrade on Tuesday when the Yugoslav federal supreme court refused to hear their claims of election fraud by the ruling socialists.

As more than 100,000 supporters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition demonstrated in the city, election commission chief Radomir Lazarevic said "all legal remedies were exhausted" by the decision.

Yugoslav Federal Interior Minister Vukasin Jokanovic warned the opposition it risked a crackdown after more than three weeks of street protests demanding the ouster of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
"Demonstrations will be crushed if protesters use force," he told Reuters.

Zajedno leaders fear police infiltrators in the daily demonstrations could provide Milosevic with an excuse to break up the demonstrations which Jokanovic admitted contained "just enough police to do their job properly".
The opposition's majority in Belgrade and other main towns was disqualified in favour of the ruling socialists for unspecified "irregularities" in the November 17 election.
Zajedno deputies boycotted the federal parliament with the support of a small Montenegrin opposition party, vowing to stay away until Milosevic admitted he cheated them of victory.
The parliament session was the first since the socialists and their allies came within reach of a two-thirds majority in federal elections on November 3.
Although the opposition did not contest the legitimacy of the federal vote, Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic said:
"Zajedno's 22 deputies will boycott all sessions of the federal parliament until the results of the (municipal) elections are recognised."
The federal election results gave Milosevic and his Montenegrin allies 84 of the 138 seats, just eight short of a two thirds majority which would allow him to change the constitution.
Political sources said Milosevic would not find it hard to muster the votes he needed among the smaller parties to force through constitutional change to keep him in power.
His term as Serbian president expires next year and there has been speculation he could become federal president after turning it into an executive post modelled on France's powerful presidency.
The running conflict over the municipal election has upset this scenario, severely denting Milosevic's electoral credibility ahead of Serbian republic elections which must be held next year.
The U.S. and other Western governments have supported the opposition, warning against the use of force and backing their demands for socialist recognition of Zajedno's win with threats of reprisals.
The United States and NATO issued separate condemnations of Milosevic on Tuesday and the alliance praised the opposition for ensuring that its demonstrations were peaceful.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in Brussels for a meeting of NATO foreign ministers, warned that if Milosevic wanted to "rule Serbia as an unreformed dictatorship, it will only increase his isolation and the suffering of his people".
The remark was read as a clear hint that Washington would back the reimposition of U.N. sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years during the war in Bosnia.
The Serbian economy is still in ruins from the last round of sanctions which mothballed industries that Milosevic has no money to revive.
But the case for sanctions is far from clear-cut and Zajedno has signalled to the West that it would oppose them.
Political sources described sanctions as a blunt instrument which would take time to have any effect and would increase the hardship of ordinary Serbs.

Independent economist Zoran Popov told Reuters on Tuesday that Milosevic could survive for a year or two with a siege economy, barter deals with Russia and China and hard-currency savings still held by Serbs.
"That way, we could still manage to increase output by some seven percent next year, albeit from a very low base," he added. "This can't go on forever but for a very long time."
